name: Chapter 13: Statistics
description: Measures of dispersion: range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation for ungrouped and grouped data, shortcut methods.

cards.term: Name the three measures of central tendency and what they tell you.
cards.definition: Mean, median, mode: a single value around which the data are centred (a “typical” value)

cards.term: Mean and median rule (ungrouped data)?
cards.definition:
\(\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum x_i}{n}\).
Median: sort the data
odd n → the ((n + 1)/2)th value
even n → the mean of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th values

cards.term: Same mean, different spread: range and standard deviation
cards.definition: Batsmen A and B both have mean=median=53, but range 117 vs 14 and SD about 36.1 vs 4.2, so B is more consistent

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Why dispersion matters

Two batsmen both average 53 with median 53. Who is more consistent, and what number shows it?

Compare how the dots are spread around 53.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Why dispersion matters

Two batsmen both average 53 with median 53. Who is more consistent, and what number shows it?

Central tendency alone is not enough. B’s scores cluster (46–60); A’s are scattered (0–117).

A single number for the spread is a measure of dispersion: range 117 vs 14; standard deviation ≈ 36.1 vs 4.2. Smaller = more consistent.

cards.term: Why are measures of central tendency not enough?
cards.definition:
Two data sets can have the same mean and median but very different scatter.
We need a number for the spread: a measure of dispersion

cards.term: Measures of dispersion in the syllabus?
cards.definition:
Range, mean deviation, variance and standard deviation.
(Quartile deviation is mentioned but not studied here.)

cards.term: Range of a data set?
cards.definition: Maximum value − minimum value. Batsman A: 117 − 0 = 117; batsman B: 60 − 46 = 14

cards.term: Limitation of the range?
cards.definition:
It uses only the two extreme values, so one outlier changes it hugely.
It says nothing about how the data spread around a central value

cards.term: Deviation of x from a?
cards.definition: x − a (signed distance). Deviations from the mean add to zero: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0, so their plain average is useless as a spread

cards.term: Why do we take absolute values of the deviations?
cards.definition:
Positive and negative deviations cancel: Σ(xᵢ − x̄) = 0
|x − a| is the actual distance on the number line, so it does not cancel

cards.term: Define mean deviation about a.
cards.definition: \(\mathrm{M.D.}(a) = \dfrac{\sum |x_i - a|}{n}\): the mean of the absolute deviations from a

cards.term: Steps to find the mean deviation about the mean/median (ungrouped)?
cards.definition: 1) Find the mean (or median) a. 2) Find |xᵢ − a| for each value. 3) Add them and divide by n

cards.term: Example 1: mean deviation about the mean of 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 4, 8, 12.
Example 2: mean deviation about the mean of the 20 data 12, 3, 18, 17, 4, 9, 17, 19, 20, 15, 8, 17, 2, 3, 16, 11, 3, 1, 0, 5.
Example 3: mean deviation about the median of 3, 9, 5, 3, 12, 10, 18, 4, 7, 19, 21.

cards.definition: Mean 10: |dev| sum 24 → 3. Mean 50: |dev| sum 84 → 8.4
Median 13.5 |dev| sum 28 → 28/12 ≈ 2.33. Median 47.5 |dev| sum 70 → 7

cards.term: Mean deviation about which point is the smallest?
cards.definition: About the median: Σ|xᵢ − a| is minimum at a = median. So M.D. about the median ≤ M.D. about the mean

cards.term: Mean deviation for a discrete frequency distribution?
cards.definition: \(\mathrm{M.D.}(\bar{x}) = \dfrac{\sum f_i|x_i - \bar{x}|}{N},\quad \bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum f_ix_i}{N},\quad N = \sum f_i\). About the median: replace x̄ by M

cards.term: Median of a discrete frequency distribution?
cards.definition: Make the cumulative frequencies. The median is the observation whose c.f. is first ≥ N/2 (if N is even, average the N/2 th and (N/2 + 1)th observations, which are often the same value)

cards.term: Method: mean deviation for a discrete distribution.
cards.definition:
1) Build a table: xᵢ, fᵢ, fᵢxᵢ (to get x̄ = Σfx/N), |xᵢ − x̄|, fᵢ|xᵢ − x̄|.
2) M.D. = Σf|x − x̄|/N.
3) Check Σf = N and that the mean lies inside the data range

cards.term: Example 5: N = 30, median = 13, Σf|xᵢ − M| = 149. Find M.D.(M).
cards.definition: 149/30 = 4.97

cards.term: Mean deviation for a continuous frequency distribution?
cards.definition: Replace each class by its mid-point, then proceed as for a discrete distribution (mean or median)

cards.term: Median of a continuous distribution: formula?
cards.definition: \(M = l + \dfrac{\frac{N}{2} - C}{f}\times h\): median class = first class with c.f. ≥ N/2; l = its lower limit, f = its frequency, h = width, C = c.f. of the preceding class

cards.term: Example 7: median of a distribution with N = 50, median class 20–30, l = 20, C = 13, f = 15, h = 10.
cards.definition: 20 + (25 − 13)/15 × 10 = 28; then Σf|xᵢ − M| = 508 → M.D.(M) = 508/50 = 10.16

cards.term: Example 6: how does the mean deviation about the mean for grouped data proceed (data 10–20 … 70–80, N = 40)?
cards.definition: x̄ = Σfx/N = 1800/40 = 45; M.D. = Σf|xᵢ − x̄|/N = 400/40 = 10

cards.term: Step-deviation (shortcut) for the mean?
cards.definition:
Take an assumed mean a and class width h: d = (x − a)/h, then
x̄ = a + h·(Σfd/N)
Only the mean uses it; the M.D. still uses |x − x̄|

cards.term: Ex 13.1 Q12: age data is given as 16–20, 21–25, …. What must you do first?
cards.definition:
Make the classes continuous before using the median formula:
subtract 0.5 from each lower limit and add 0.5 to each upper limit
(15.5–20.5, 20.5–25.5, …)

cards.term: Limitations of the mean deviation?
cards.definition: About the median it is unreliable when variability is very high about the mean it is less “scientific” and since it uses |·| it cannot be treated algebraically → we need the standard deviation

cards.term: Why not use Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² directly as the dispersion?
cards.definition: It grows with the number of observations: set A (6 values, spread 5–55) has sum of squares 1750 while set B (31 values, 15–45) has 2480, even though A is more scattered. So we take the mean

cards.term: Define the variance σ² of n observations.
cards.definition: \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(x_i - \bar{x})^2\): the mean of the squared deviations from the mean

cards.term: Define the standard deviation.
cards.definition: \(\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n}\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2}\): the positive square root of the variance; it has the same unit as the data

cards.term: Set A: 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55 versus set B: 15, 16, …, 45. Compare σ².
cards.definition: A: 1750/6 ≈ 291.67. B: 2480/31 = 80. A is far more dispersed (both have mean 30)

cards.term: Computational formula for variance?
cards.definition: \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{\sum x_i^2}{n} - \bar{x}^2\): mean of squares minus square of the mean. Faster and less error-prone

cards.term: Example 8: variance and SD of 6, 8, 10, …, 24.
cards.definition: x̄ = 15; Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 330; σ² = 33, σ = 5.74

cards.term: Discrete frequency distribution: variance formula?
cards.definition: \(\sigma^2 = \dfrac{1}{N}\sum f_i(x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \dfrac{\sum f_ix_i^2}{N} - \left(\dfrac{\sum f_ix_i}{N}\right)^2\)

cards.term: Example 9: N = 30, Σfx = 420, Σf(x − x̄)² = 1374. Find the mean, variance, SD.
cards.definition: x̄ = 14, σ² = 1374/30 = 45.8, σ ≈ 6.77

cards.term: Standard deviation of a continuous distribution?
cards.definition: Use the class mid-points xᵢ as in a discrete distribution: σ = (1/N)√(NΣfx² − (Σfx)²)

cards.term: Example 10: the table with mid-points 35 … 95: Σfx = 3100, Σf(x − x̄)² = 10050, N = 50.
cards.definition: x̄ = 62, σ² = 201, σ = 14.18

cards.term: Grouped data: mean 62, variance 201, SD 14.18
cards.definition: Classes 30-100 with f=3,7,12,15,8,3,2: mean 62, variance 201, SD ≈ 14.18

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Example 10 · mean and standard deviation

Frequencies 3, 7, 12, 15, 8, 3, 2 on classes 30–40 … 90–100. Find the mean, variance and standard deviation.

Use class mid-points and the frequencies.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Example 10 · mean and standard deviation

Frequencies 3, 7, 12, 15, 8, 3, 2 on classes 30–40 … 90–100. Find the mean, variance and standard deviation.

Mid-points 35, 45, …, 95. Σfx = 3100, N = 50 → x̄ = 62. Σf(x − x̄)² = 10050 → variance = 201, σ = √201 ≈ 14.18.

Most of the data lies within x̄ ± σ (the shaded band). σ has the same unit as the data; variance has the square of the unit.

cards.term: Example 11: N = 48, Σfx = 614 and Σfx² = 9652. Find the standard deviation.
Shortcut method for variance and SD?
cards.definition: Let y = (x − A)/h. Then σ² = h²[Σfy²/N − (Σfy/N)²], σ = h·√(Σfy²/N − (Σfy/N)²), and x̄ = A + h·Σfy/N

cards.term: Example 12 (shortcut): A = 65, h = 10, N = 50, Σfy = −15, Σfy² = 105 for the data of Example 10. Find mean, variance, SD.
cards.definition: x̄ = 65 + 10(−15/50) = 62 σ² = 100[105/50 − (−0.3)²] = 201 σ = 14.18. Same as Example 10

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q1: mean and variance of 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 4, 8, 12.
cards.definition: x̄ = 9; Σ(x − 9)² = 74 → σ² = 9.25

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q2–3: mean and variance of the first n natural numbers; of the first 10 multiples of 3.
cards.definition: Mean (n + 1)/2, variance (n² − 1)/12. Multiples of 3: mean 16.5, variance 9 × 99/12 = 74.25

cards.term: Variance of the first n terms of any A.P. with common difference d?
cards.definition: d²(n² − 1)/12 (the general form of the previous card)

cards.term: Interpretation: small vs large σ?
cards.definition:
Small σ: data close to the mean (consistent, uniform).
Large σ: data scattered. σ = 0 iff every observation equals the mean

cards.term: Ex 13.2 Q9–10: what to do for the diameters 33–36, 37–40, …?
cards.definition:
The classes have gaps.
1) Make them continuous using half the gap (32.5–36.5, 36.5–40.5, …).
2) Use mid-points and the shortcut method

cards.term: Effect of shift and scale on mean and variance
cards.definition: y=x+a: mean shifts by a, variance unchanged; y=kx: mean×k, variance×k², SD×|k|; y=ax+b gives SD |a|σ

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Change of origin and scale

Add 4 to every observation; separately multiply every observation by 2. What happens to the mean and the variance?

Does the spread change when everything slides?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Change of origin and scale

Add 4 to every observation; separately multiply every observation by 2. What happens to the mean and the variance?

Shift (x + a): mean + a, variance unchanged (spread unaffected). Scale (kx): mean × k, variance × k², SD × |k|.

Together: for y = ax + b, ȳ = a x̄ + b, σ_y = |a| σ_x. (Examples 13 and 15.)

cards.term: Example 13: the variance of 20 observations is 5. Each is multiplied by 2. New variance?
cards.definition: 20 (variance × 2² = 5 × 4). SD becomes 2σ

cards.term: Example 15: each observation is increased by a. Effect on variance?
cards.definition: None: variance unchanged (mean also shifts by a, so deviations stay the same)

cards.term: Effect of y = ax + b on mean, variance, SD?
cards.definition: ȳ = a x̄ + b, σ_y² = a²σ_x², σ_y = |a|σ_x

cards.term: Example 14: mean of 5 observations is 4.4, variance 8.24; three are 1, 2, 6. Find the others.
cards.definition: x + y = 13 and x² + y² = 97 → (x − y)² = 25 → 4 and 9

cards.term: Example 16: 100 observations, mean 40 and σ = 5.1, but one value 40 was recorded as 50. Correct mean and σ.
cards.definition: Correct sum 4000 − 50 + 40 = 3990 → mean 39.9; Σx² = 162601 − 2500 + 1600 = 161701 → σ = 5

cards.term: Method: correcting a wrong observation.
cards.definition:
Recompute Σx and Σx² by removing the wrong value and adding the right one.
Σx² = n(σ² + x̄²) gives the old sum of squares

cards.term: Misc Q1: 8 observations, mean 9, variance 9.25; six are 6, 7, 10, 12, 12, 13. Find the other two.
cards.definition: x + y = 12 and x² + y² = 80 → 4 and 8

cards.term: Misc Q2: 7 observations, mean 8, variance 16; five are 2, 4, 10, 12, 14. Find the other two.
cards.definition: x + y = 14 and x² + y² = 100 → 6 and 8

cards.term: Misc Q3: mean 8 and SD 4 for six observations, each multiplied by 3. New mean and SD?
cards.definition: 24 and 12

cards.term: Misc Q4: prove that ax₁, …, axₙ have mean a x̄ and variance a²σ².
cards.definition: Mean = Σax/n = a x̄; deviations become a(x − x̄), so squares × a²: variance a²σ² ✓

cards.term:
Misc Q5: 20 observations, mean 10, σ = 2; one value 8 was wrong. Correct mean and σ if
(i) omitted
(ii) replaced by 12.
cards.definition: (i) 19 values: sum 192, Σx² = 2016 → mean 10.11, σ ≈ 2.0. (ii) sum 204, Σx² = 2160 → mean 10.2, σ ≈ 1.99

cards.term: Misc Q6: 100 observations, mean 20, σ = 3; three incorrect values 21, 21, 18 are omitted. New mean and σ?
cards.definition: Sum 2000 − 60 = 1940 over 97 values → mean 20; Σx² = 40900 − 1206 = 39694 → σ ≈ 3.04

cards.term: Coefficient of variation (compare consistency of two data sets)?
cards.definition: \(\mathrm{C.V.} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\bar{x}}\times 100\%\). The set with the smaller C.V. is more consistent

cards.term: Series A: mean 50, σ = 5. Series B: mean 80, σ = 6. Which is more consistent?
cards.definition: C.V. (A) = 10%, C.V. (B) = 7.5% → B is more consistent (its σ is smaller relative to its mean)

cards.term: Combined mean and variance of two groups (n₁, x̄₁, σ₁²), (n₂, x̄₂, σ₂²)?
cards.definition:
Combined mean (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂)
Combined variance [n₁(σ₁² + d₁²) + n₂(σ₂² + d₂²)]/(n₁ + n₂)
with dᵢ = x̄ᵢ − x̄_combined

cards.term: Empirical relation between mean, median, mode?
cards.definition: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean (for moderately skewed data)

cards.term: Weighted mean?
cards.definition: \(\dfrac{\sum w_ix_i}{\sum w_i}\): e.g. exam components with weights 20%, 30%, 50%

cards.term: Mean of an A.P. and of the first n natural numbers?
cards.definition:
The mean of an A.P. is the average of its first and last terms (= the middle term)
First n natural numbers: (n + 1)/2

cards.term: Sum of squared deviations from a: which a minimises Σ(x − a)²? Which minimises Σ|x − a|?
cards.definition: Σ(x − a)² is minimum at a = mean (and the minimum value is nσ²). Σ|x − a| is minimum at a = median

cards.term: Variance of n identical observations? Of two values a and b?
cards.definition: 0 and ((b − a)/2)² (SD = half the difference)

cards.term: Relation: Σ(xᵢ − a)² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² + n(x̄ − a)². Why useful?
cards.definition:
It shows the sum of squares about any a exceeds the one about the mean by n(x̄ − a)².
Handy for the assumed-mean method and for proving that the mean minimises it
20 − 3 = (b) 17

cards.term:
MCQ: The mean deviation about the mean of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is
(a) 2.4 (b) 2 (c) 3 (d) 6
cards.definition: Mean 6; |dev| 4, 2, 0, 2, 4 = 12 → 12/5 = (a) 2.4

cards.term:
MCQ: The variance of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 is
(a) 6 (b) 8 (c) 10 (d) 40
cards.definition: Σ(x − 6)² = 40 → (b) 8

cards.term:
MCQ: If the SD of a set is 4, the variance is
(a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 8 (d) 16
cards.definition: (d) 16

cards.term:
MCQ: If each observation is multiplied by 3, the SD becomes
(a) σ (b) 3σ (c) 9σ (d) σ + 3
cards.definition: (b) 3σ

cards.term:
MCQ: Each observation is increased by 5. Then the variance
(a) increases by 5 (b) increases by 25 (c) is unchanged (d) is multiplied by 5
cards.definition: (c)

cards.term:
MCQ: The standard deviation of the first 10 natural numbers is
(a) √8.25 (b) 2.87 (c) 3.03 (d) both (a) and (b)

MCQ: The sum of deviations of the observations from their mean is
(a) always positive (b) always negative (c) zero (d) depends on n
cards.definition: (c) zero

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): the variance of the first 10 natural numbers is σ². Find 12σ².
cards.definition: σ² = (n² − 1)/12 = 99/12 → 12σ² = 99

cards.term: Integer answer: mean of 5 observations is 6 and Σx² = 200. Find 5 × variance.
cards.definition: σ² = 200/5 − 36 = 4 → 5σ² = 20

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: The standard deviation is never negative.
R: It is the positive square root of the variance.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: Adding 10 to every observation leaves the standard deviation unchanged.
R: Dispersion depends only on the deviations from the mean, not on the location of the mean.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term: True/False: the mean deviation about the mean is always less than or equal to the standard deviation.
cards.definition: True: M.D. ≤ σ (by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality). Equality only if all |deviations| are equal

cards.term: 3-mark: find the variance of 5, 12, 3, 18, 45, 9.
4-mark: two firms: A pays mean ₹520 with σ = ₹100; B pays mean ₹495 with σ = ₹80. Which has more uniform wages?
cards.definition: C.V. (A) = 100/520 × 100 ≈ 19.2%; C.V. (B) = 80/495 × 100 ≈ 16.2% → B is more uniform

cards.term: Case-based: test scores of a class: mean 62, standard deviation 14.18 (Example 10). About which range do most students lie?
cards.definition: About x̄ ± σ = 47.8 to 76.2 (roughly two-thirds of students for bell-shaped data)
